sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Cáer, also recorded as Cáer Ibormeith, is an Irish figure named a heroine or a goddess. The god of poetry, Aonghus Óg, dreamed of a woman he had never met. His desire grew so strong that he wandered the world in search of her. At last he came to the Lake of Dragon's Mouths. There he found Cáer swimming in the form of a swan. The swan was decked with one hundred and thirty golden chains. Aonghus turned himself into a swan and joined her. The pair flew off together and sang so sweet that all who heard them slept for three days and nights. The poet William Yeats used this tale for his poem the Song of Wandering Aengus.

okr.objective: Cáer is a swan maiden beloved of the poet god Aonghus.
key_results: Cáer is a heroine or goddess of Irish legend.
Aonghus the god of poetry searched the world for her.
He met her as a swan on the Lake of Dragon's Mouths.
The pair flew away together and their song brought sleep.
